metadata.title: Double Jump Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Double Jump Bottom position in BJJ. Dynamic entry to deep half guard with explosive sweeps and back takes. Advanced guard recovery technique with 65% sweep success rate.

overview:
Double Jump Bottom is an advanced dynamic entry position used to recover guard and transition into deep half guard when under pressure from top control. This explosive technique involves shooting both legs underneath the opponent's hips while on your side, creating a brief airborne moment before establishing deep half hooks. The position is particularly effective against heavy pressure passing and allows the bottom player to quickly transition from a defensive scenario to an offensive deep half guard system.

The Double Jump Bottom position represents a modern approach to guard recovery that prioritizes dynamic movement over static frames. Unlike traditional elbow escapes that rely on incremental hip movement, the double jump commits fully to explosive leg insertion, making it difficult for opponents to predict and counter. This position is foundational in Eddie Bravo's 10th Planet system and has been refined by competitors like Geo Martinez and Richie Martinez to create devastating sweep and back-take chains.

Successful execution of Double Jump Bottom requires precise timing, explosive hip mobility, and the ability to read your opponent's weight distribution. When executed properly, it bypasses traditional passing defenses and immediately places you in an advantageous deep half position with multiple offensive options including the old school sweep, electric chair, and waiter sweep sequences.
state_invariants: Bottom player's body positioned on their side with hips oriented perpendicular to opponent's centerline, creating the angle necessary for leg insertion underneath opponent's base
Both of bottom player's legs actively shooting underneath opponent's hips in synchronized motion, with knees driving toward opponent's far hip while feet hook behind near leg
Top player's weight distributed forward over bottom player's torso, creating the pressure that makes the explosive entry possible through their commitment to the pass
Bottom player's upper body maintains defensive frames with arms protecting against crossface and controlling opponent's near arm to prevent base recovery
Bottom player's head positioned away from opponent's hips on the outside, maintaining safe distance from potential submission attacks while creating the leverage angle for the sweep entries
prerequisites: Opponent applying forward pressure from top position (side control, headquarters, or knee slice)
Bottom player has inside space to initiate hip movement
Top player's weight committed forward rather than posting back
Bottom player positioned on their side rather than flat on back
Sufficient hip mobility to execute explosive leg insertion
Timing window when opponent's base is compromised
key_principles: Explosive hip extension is critical - the jump must be committed and fast to prevent opponent from sprawling back
Both legs must shoot simultaneously underneath opponent's hips to create the destabilizing effect
Maintain angle of your body perpendicular to opponent's centerline throughout the entry
Use opponent's forward pressure against them - the harder they pressure, the more effective the entry
Immediately establish deep half hooks after entry to secure position before opponent can recover base
Keep head outside and away from opponent's hips to avoid guillotine and other front headlock attacks
Control opponent's near arm during entry to prevent posting and base recovery

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent sprawls legs back - immediately establish deep half hooks on their near leg
Opponent steps over to avoid sweep - follow their movement and take the back
Opponent tries to flatten you out - lock down their leg and initiate sweep sequence
Opponent stands up to avoid deep half - transition legs to X-Guard configuration
Opponent commits weight forward to crossface - use underhook to sweep

decision_tree.condition: If opponent's weight is heavily committed forward and their base is narrow
Else if opponent sprawls legs back and widens base to defend
Else if opponent stands up to create distance
Else if opponent attempts to step over your legs
Else if opponent applies heavy crossface pressure

common_errors.error: Jumping with legs at different timing or angles
common_errors.consequence: Creates predictable movement that opponent can easily sprawl against, resulting in flattened position under heavy pressure
common_errors.correction: Practice the synchronized double leg insertion in drilling - both legs must shoot together like a single explosive unit, maintaining parallel alignment throughout the motion

common_errors.error: Failing to commit fully to the explosive entry movement
common_errors.consequence: Halfway attempts allow opponent to post and recover base, leaving you in worse position than before the attempt
common_errors.correction: The double jump requires full commitment - once initiated, drive both legs completely underneath opponent's hips with maximum explosiveness, accepting the risk to gain the reward

common_errors.error: Allowing head to drift toward opponent's hips during entry
common_errors.consequence: Creates guillotine and other front headlock attack opportunities that can end the match immediately
common_errors.correction: Actively turn head away from opponent's hips toward the outside, maintaining safe head position while establishing deep half hooks

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control opponent's near arm during transition
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to post and recover base, nullifying the sweeping opportunities from deep half
common_errors.correction: Establish control of opponent's near arm with your outside hand before initiating the jump, preventing their ability to post during your entry

common_errors.error: Attempting the technique against opponent with weight posted back
common_errors.consequence: Without forward pressure, the explosive entry has nothing to work against and you expose yourself to leg attacks
common_errors.correction: Only execute double jump when opponent's weight is clearly committed forward - use other guard recovery methods when they maintain back-posted base

common_errors.error: Stopping movement after successful entry without establishing hooks
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately escapes before you can consolidate deep half position
common_errors.correction: The entry and hook establishment must be one continuous motion - as legs shoot underneath, immediately curl the inside leg to hook opponent's far leg while outside leg controls near hip

common_errors.error: Executing from flat on back instead of on side
common_errors.consequence: Lacks the angular momentum and leverage needed for explosive leg insertion
common_errors.correction: Always establish side position first with body perpendicular to opponent before initiating the double jump sequence

training_drills.name: Static Entry Repetition Drill
training_drills.description: Partner maintains heavy top pressure from side control or headquarters position. Bottom player executes 10 consecutive double jump entries, focusing on synchronized leg insertion and immediate deep half hook establishment. Reset to starting position after each repetition. Emphasize explosive hip extension and proper head positioning throughout.

training_drills.name: Flow Rolling from Double Jump
training_drills.description: Start in double jump bottom position with partner applying moderate resistance. Bottom player attempts to transition to deep half and execute sweeps while top player defends at 50-70% intensity. Focus on chaining techniques together (deep half entry → old school sweep → back take) rather than completing individual moves. Switch roles every 3 minutes.

training_drills.name: Timing Development Drill
training_drills.description: Top player moves between knee slice, headquarters, and side control pressure positions randomly. Bottom player must recognize the optimal timing window when opponent's weight commits forward and execute double jump entry. Partner provides verbal feedback on timing quality. Emphasize reading opponent's weight distribution and reacting explosively to opportunities.

training_drills.name: Counter Response Chain Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player successfully enters double jump position. Top player then applies one of four defensive responses (sprawl, base widen, crossface, or stand up) while bottom player must execute appropriate counter technique. Partner calls out defense type for first 3 minutes, then applies randomly for remaining time. Focus on automatic recognition and response patterns.

training_drills.name: Progressive Resistance Double Jump
training_drills.description: Partner starts with zero resistance, allowing perfect execution of double jump to deep half to sweep sequence. Gradually increase resistance over 10-minute period from 0% to 80%, forcing bottom player to maintain technical precision under increasing pressure. Emphasizes building confidence and technical soundness before adding intensity.

expert_insights.danaher: The double jump represents a critical paradigm shift in guard recovery methodology - rather than incrementally creating space through traditional shrimping mechanics, we commit entirely to explosive leg insertion that bypasses the opponent's passing structure in a single motion. The biomechanical efficiency of this technique lies in converting the opponent's forward pressure into the very force that enables your leg insertion. When they drive their weight onto your torso, they create a pivot point around which your hips can rotate explosively. The key technical element often missed by practitioners is the necessity of maintaining perpendicular body alignment throughout the entry - your torso must remain on its side with the shoulder line at ninety degrees to the opponent's centerline. This geometric relationship is what allows both legs to shoot underneath their hips simultaneously rather than sequentially, which would telegraph the movement and allow defensive sprawling. The position also exemplifies the concept of position before submission - while the electric chair and banana split are tempting immediate attacks, the higher percentage pathway involves first consolidating deep half guard control, then using the opponent's defensive reactions to create the submission openings.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the double jump is one of the highest-percentage guard recovery techniques when you're getting smashed in bottom half or headquarters positions. I use this constantly against guys who are trying to pressure pass me because it completely nullifies their forward pressure strategy - the harder they drive into you, the better the entry works. The timing aspect is crucial though - you can't just randomly throw your legs under whenever you want. You need to wait for that specific moment when their weight commits forward and their hands are occupied trying to control your upper body. That's when you explode with the double jump and they have zero time to react. Once you establish the deep half hooks, you immediately have access to multiple high-level sweeps - old school, waiter, homer simpson - and if they defend those, you're taking the back. The competition proven sequence is double jump to deep half, opponent defends the sweep by stepping over, you roll under and take the back. This works at the highest levels because the defensive responses to deep half sweeps are predictable and you can have your counter programmed before they even make their move. The electric chair is also there as a finishing option when guys get stubborn and refuse to give up the position.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The double jump is pure 10th Planet innovation - we developed this because traditional guard recovery was too slow and predictable against modern pressure passing. When someone's crushing you with that knee slice or headquarters pressure, you don't have time to frame and shrimp incrementally like it's 1995. You need to create chaos and explode into a dominant position immediately, and that's exactly what double jump does. The technique is all about that explosive entry where both legs shoot under at the same time - it's like a double leg takedown but you're doing it upside down and backwards. Once you're in that deep half position, you've got the whole system available: lockdown to electric chair, old school sweep to mount, waiter sweep to side control, or you can transition to dogfight and take the back. The beautiful thing is your opponent can't really train to defend it effectively because the entry is so fast and unexpected. By the time they realize what's happening, you've already got your hooks in and you're attacking. We drill this constantly at 10th Planet gyms because it's a position that gives smaller guys the ability to sweep much bigger opponents using timing and explosion rather than trying to muscle them around. The electric chair finish from here is also one of my favorite submissions because it attacks the hip and knee simultaneously, creating a pain compliance scenario that's really hard to tough out even for the most stubborn competitors.

overview: Double Jump is an advanced half guard top position characterized by the top player establishing double underhooks while the bottom player maintains the half guard lock. This position represents a critical control point in the half guard passing sequence, where the top practitioner has significantly neutralized the bottom player's offensive capabilities while maintaining pressure and advancement options. The position derives its name from the jumping motion often used to secure the second underhook, creating a powerful controlling configuration that limits the bottom player's mobility and frame-building capacity. Double Jump is particularly prevalent in high-level no-gi grappling and represents a key transitional state between standard half guard top and complete passing positions. The configuration allows for systematic pressure application, shoulder-of-justice control, and multiple high-percentage passing sequences while simultaneously shutting down common half guard sweeps and back-take attempts.
state_invariants: Top player has both arms secured in underhook position on the bottom player's torso, with hands typically clasped together or gripping opponent's far hip/lat, creating a locked controlling frame that prevents bottom player from establishing defensive frames or creating distance

Bottom player's leg configuration maintains half guard lock around top player's trapped leg, with foot typically locked at or above the knee, preventing immediate leg extraction while bottom player works for recovery or escape

Top player's chest pressure drives downward and forward into bottom player's upper body, with head positioned low on the trapped-leg side to prevent opponent from achieving underhook or establishing effective frames, while hips stay heavy and connected to opponent's lower body

Bottom player's arm positioning is compromised with both arms typically unable to establish underhooks due to top player's double underhook control, forcing reliance on frames against top player's head or attempts to break grip connections

Weight distribution from top player creates forward pressure through the chest and shoulder into bottom player's head and upper torso, while hips remain heavy on the trapped leg side, limiting bottom player's ability to create angles or generate sweeping momentum
prerequisites: Top player has achieved at least one underhook from half guard top position
Bottom player is on their side or back with half guard established
Top player has sufficient grip control to secure second underhook
Bottom player's defensive frames have been compromised or neutralized
Top player's trapped leg is controlled but passing sequence is viable
key_principles: Maintain heavy chest pressure driving through both underhooks to flatten opponent and limit their mobility
Keep head positioned low on trapped-leg side to prevent opponent from securing underhook or building effective frames
Control opponent's far hip or lat with underhook grips to prevent them from turning away or creating distance
Apply shoulder-of-justice pressure into opponent's face/jaw to create discomfort and disrupt their defensive structure
Maintain tight connection between your hips and opponent's lower body to prevent them from creating space for escape sequences
Systematically work to free trapped leg through small movements while maintaining upper body control and pressure
Transition between passing attacks based on opponent's defensive reactions while keeping double underhook control intact

Opponent turns away to escape underhook control
Opponent flattens out or loses half guard lock temporarily

Opponent attempts to recover guard or create angles

Else if opponent turns away attempting to escape underhook control

common_errors.error: Allowing head position to rise too high, giving opponent space to establish frames or underhook
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player recovers defensive structure and can initiate sweeps or back-takes, neutralizing passing advantage
common_errors.correction: Keep head low and tight to trapped-leg side, driving shoulder pressure into opponent's jaw/face to maintain control and prevent frame-building

common_errors.error: Losing tight connection between hips and opponent's lower body, creating space
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can create angles for sweeps, recover full guard, or transition to deep half guard
common_errors.correction: Maintain heavy hip pressure on trapped leg side, keeping your hips glued to opponent's lower body throughout passing sequences

common_errors.error: Releasing underhook control prematurely before establishing alternative grips or control points
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately establishes underhook or frames, recovering defensive position and sweep opportunities
common_errors.correction: Only release underhooks when transitioning to specific passing grips (crossface, far hip, etc.) and ensure alternative control is secured first

common_errors.error: Attempting to free trapped leg through explosive movements without maintaining upper body control
common_errors.consequence: Compromises pressure and balance, allowing opponent to capitalize with sweeps or reversals
common_errors.correction: Free trapped leg through gradual movements and weight shifts while maintaining constant chest pressure and double underhook control

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's far hip or lat with underhook grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can turn away, create distance, or transition to more advantageous positions like deep half guard
common_errors.correction: Ensure at least one underhook actively controls far hip or lat, preventing opponent from creating angles or escaping pressure

common_errors.error: Staying static in double underhook position without working toward pass completion
common_errors.consequence: Opponent has time to develop lockdown, recover defensive structure, or attempt submission attacks
common_errors.correction: Continuously advance toward pass completion using small adjustments, weight shifts, and systematic pressure application rather than holding static position

training_drills.name: Double Underhook Entry and Maintenance
training_drills.description: Starting from standard half guard top with one underhook, practice jumping to secure second underhook while maintaining pressure. Partner provides light resistance. Focus on maintaining chest pressure and head position throughout the transition. Work both from static positions and during live half guard sequences.

training_drills.name: Passing Sequence Flow from Double Jump
training_drills.description: Begin in established double jump position. Work through systematic passing sequence: shoulder pressure, knee slice attempt, adapt to partner's defensive reaction (frame, turn away, turtle), execute appropriate counter-transition. Partner provides progressive resistance increasing from 50% to 80% over rounds.

training_drills.name: Double Jump Retention Against Escapes
training_drills.description: Partner starts in double jump bottom position and attempts common escapes: building frames, recovering underhook, transitioning to deep half, lockdown attacks. Top player must maintain double underhook control and pressure while defending against each escape attempt. Switch roles every round.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring: Half Guard to Pass
training_drills.description: Start from standard half guard top position. Top player's goal is to achieve double jump and complete pass within the round. Bottom player works to prevent double underhooks or escape if achieved. Reset to half guard top when pass is completed or bottom player escapes to neutral. Track success rate of achieving double jump and pass completion.

expert_insights.danaher: The double jump configuration represents a critical control point in the systematic dismantling of half guard defenses. What makes this position theoretically significant is the complete neutralization of the bottom player's primary defensive weapon: their ability to build frames and create distance. By establishing double underhooks, you have eliminated both of your opponent's arms as defensive tools, forcing them to rely solely on their leg control, which is insufficient against proper pressure application. The key mechanical principle here is understanding that this is not a static holding position but rather a transitional control state that must be leveraged immediately for passing advancement. Your chest pressure must be constant and forward-driving, creating a compression effect that flattens your opponent and limits their hip mobility. The position of your head is absolutely critical—it must remain low on the trapped-leg side, using shoulder-of-justice pressure into the opponent's jaw to prevent them from building any upper body frames. From this configuration, your passing sequences become highly systematic: if they flatten, execute the knee slice; if they turn away, take the back; if they turtle, attack the neck. The position's power lies not in its holding capacity but in the way it forces your opponent into a limited set of defensive options, each of which leads to a predetermined offensive response.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Double jump is one of the highest-percentage positions I use in competition because it puts your opponent in an absolute nightmare scenario where all their best options are shut down. In high-level matches, when you secure double underhooks from half guard, you're basically telling your opponent they're about to get passed—it's just a question of which direction and how much they're going to suffer in the process. The competition reality is that most guys will try to turn away when you establish this control, and that's exactly when you step over and take the back for easy points and submission opportunities. If they're smart and stay flat, you just drive that shoulder into their face until they can't breathe properly, then slice through for the pass. What makes this position so effective at the highest levels is that it completely removes the bottom player's ability to create the chaos and scrambles that modern half guard is built on. No frames means no distance, no distance means no sweeps, no sweeps means you're just methodically breaking them down. I've finished matches from this position hundreds of times, and the pattern is always the same: establish the double underhooks, apply suffocating pressure, wait for their defensive reaction, then capitalize with the appropriate pass or back take. The only real danger is if you get lazy with your pressure and let them recover an underhook or transition to deep half, which is why you need to be constantly advancing, never just holding.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: From the 10th Planet perspective, double jump is what we're trying to prevent at all costs when we're on bottom, because it shuts down basically everything in our half guard game. Once someone gets double underhooks on you, your lockdown becomes way less effective, you can't really build toward old school, and all your sweeping mechanics are compromised. But when you're on top and you secure it, man, you've basically won that positional battle, especially in no-gi where there's no collar grips to help the bottom guy. The key thing I teach my guys when they get this position is to immediately start hunting for the darce or anaconda if the opponent does what most people do and turtles up to escape the pressure. That head and arm position is right there, and if you've already got the double underhooks, transitioning to the darce is super smooth. The other thing that's slick from here is if they're staying flat and defensive, you can use that shoulder pressure to set up some nasty gi-less baseball chokes or just grind them down until they make a mistake. The position itself isn't traditionally part of our bottom game, but when we're on top, it's money because it neutralizes all those rubber guard and lockdown attacks that give most top players problems. Just don't get too comfortable holding it—keep advancing, keep attacking, because a good lockdown player will eventually find a way to create some chaos if you let them hang around too long.

metadata.title: Double Jump Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Double Jump Top position in BJJ. Advanced turtle attack with leg hooks creating back control opportunities. Success rates: Beginner 25%, Intermediate 45%, Advanced 65%.

overview:
Double Jump Top is an advanced attacking position from turtle where the top practitioner establishes bilateral leg hooks (both legs hooking inside the opponent's thighs) while maintaining upper body control. This dynamic position creates immediate back-taking opportunities and represents a transitional state between turtle top control and full back control. The position gets its name from the explosive 'jumping' motion used to establish both hooks simultaneously, though it can also be entered progressively.

The strategic value of Double Jump Top lies in its ability to bypass traditional turtle defenses and create immediate submission threats. By controlling the opponent's hips with leg hooks while maintaining upper body pressure through harness grips or crossface control, the top player eliminates the bottom player's base and forces defensive reactions. This position is particularly effective in no-gi competition where traditional collar grips are unavailable, and leg entanglement becomes the primary control mechanism.

Double Jump Top represents modern turtle attack methodology, emphasizing leg-based controls over purely upper-body attacks. The position creates a powerful dilemma: if the opponent attempts to address the leg hooks, they expose their back; if they defend their back, the leg hooks can be used to off-balance and sweep. This dual-threat nature makes Double Jump Top a high-percentage entry to back control against skilled defensive grapplers who excel at defending traditional turtle attacks.
state_invariants: Top practitioner's legs hooked inside bottom opponent's thighs bilaterally, with feet controlling hip positioning and preventing base recovery
Top practitioner maintains upper body control through harness grips (seatbelt), crossface, or overhook positioning to prevent opponent's escape to guard
Bottom opponent remains in turtle base position (hands and knees) but with compromised hip control due to leg hooks eliminating lower body stability
Top practitioner's chest pressure directed into opponent's upper back or shoulder region, creating forward and downward weight distribution
Bottom opponent's defensive posture attempts to maintain hand-knee base while managing dual threats of back exposure and sweep vulnerability
prerequisites: Opponent in defensive turtle position with hands and knees on mat
Top practitioner has positional dominance from previous guard pass, scramble, or turtle attack
Sufficient space and timing to establish first leg hook without immediate counter
Upper body control established (crossface, overhook, or head control) before leg hook insertion
Opponent's defensive focus directed toward traditional turtle defense rather than leg hook prevention
key_principles: Establish leg hooks progressively or explosively depending on opponent's base strength and defensive awareness
Maintain constant upper body pressure to prevent opponent sitting to guard or rolling through escapes
Use leg hooks to control opponent's hips and eliminate base rather than as static positioning
Create immediate back-taking opportunities by transitioning hooks from inside position to traditional back control hooks
Balance weight distribution between chest pressure and hook control to prevent opponent's defensive rolls
Anticipate and counter opponent's attempt to sit to butterfly guard by redirecting to back control
Maintain offensive initiative by chaining attacks between back-takes, crab rides, and truck positions

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to sit to butterfly guard or turn into you
Opponent tries to roll away from pressure while you maintain hook control
Opponent commits to forward roll escape while you follow rotation with hooks
Opponent flattens to belly attempting to defend leg hooks

decision_tree.condition: If opponent maintains strong turtle base and resists hook insertion
If opponent attempts to sit to butterfly guard or turn into you
If opponent rolls away from pressure to escape hooks
If opponent flattens to belly to defend hooks

common_errors.error: Establishing leg hooks without securing upper body control first
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily sits to butterfly guard or rolls through to reverse position, eliminating attacking opportunities
common_errors.correction: Always secure crossface, overhook, or harness grip before inserting hooks; upper body control prevents defensive movements

common_errors.error: Using leg hooks as static positioning rather than active control mechanisms
common_errors.consequence: Opponent maintains base and stalls position, or gradually extracts hooks through patient defensive work
common_errors.correction: Constantly adjust hook depth and angle to off-balance opponent; use hooks to lift and manipulate hips, not just maintain contact

common_errors.error: Overcommitting weight forward onto opponent's back without maintaining base
common_errors.consequence: Opponent performs forward roll escape, throwing you over their head and reversing position
common_errors.correction: Distribute weight between chest pressure and leg control; maintain your own base to follow opponent's movements without being thrown

common_errors.error: Failing to anticipate opponent sitting to butterfly guard and losing position
common_errors.consequence: Opponent establishes butterfly hooks and sweeps or creates scramble, negating your attacking position
common_errors.correction: As opponent begins sitting motion, immediately transition to crab ride or back control, using their movement to establish dominant position

common_errors.error: Inserting both hooks simultaneously without regard for opponent's defensive reactions
common_errors.consequence: Opponent counters the explosive entry with roll escapes or by posting and standing, creating scramble situations
common_errors.correction: Read opponent's base strength; against strong turtle, establish hooks progressively while breaking down base incrementally

common_errors.error: Maintaining Double Jump position for extended periods seeking perfect back-take setup
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers defensive composure, extracts hooks, or referee stands up position for stalling
common_errors.correction: Use Double Jump as transitional attacking position; commit to back-take, truck entry, or submission within 5-10 seconds of establishing hooks

training_drills.name: Progressive Hook Insertion Drill
training_drills.description: Partner maintains defensive turtle while you practice inserting first hook, establishing control, then adding second hook. Partner provides 50% resistance, gradually increasing to 75% as technique improves. Focus on maintaining upper body control throughout hook insertion sequence. Drill both progressive insertion (one hook at a time) and explosive double hook entry. 5 minutes per side.

training_drills.name: Back-Take Flow Drill from Double Jump
training_drills.description: Starting from established Double Jump position, practice transitioning to back control, crab ride, and truck positions based on partner's defensive reactions. Partner cycles through sitting to guard, rolling away, and flattening defenses while you read and respond with appropriate transitions. Emphasize smooth flow between positions without stopping. 8 minutes continuous flow.

training_drills.name: Double Jump Positional Sparring
training_drills.description: Start each round with you in Double Jump Top position with both hooks established. Partner's goal is to escape to guard or standing within 2 minutes. Your goal is to advance to back control, truck, or crab ride. Reset after each successful advancement or escape. Compete 5 rounds to develop timing and transition recognition under resistance. Track success rate of transitions versus escapes.

expert_insights.danaher: The Double Jump position represents a sophisticated understanding of control hierarchy in ground fighting. The bilateral hook insertion creates what I term 'base negation through hip control' - by eliminating the opponent's ability to post their legs effectively, you remove their primary defensive tool from turtle. The critical mechanical insight is that leg hooks function not merely as points of contact, but as leverage systems that allow inferior upper body position to generate superior control outcomes. Notice how the Double Jump position inverts traditional turtle attack methodology: rather than seeking upper body dominance first, you establish lower body control that forces upper body compliance. This is biomechanically efficient because the opponent's defensive energy must be divided between preventing back exposure and maintaining base, creating the classical dilemma structure. The position's transitional nature is not a weakness but a feature - it exists as a forcing mechanism that compels opponent reactions, each of which opens specific attacking pathways. The key technical detail that separates competent from expert execution is hook depth and angle variation: your hooks must actively manipulate the opponent's hip positioning, not simply occupy space inside their legs.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Double Jump is one of those positions that looks wild but actually gives you massive control if you hit it right. I use this constantly in competition when guys turtle up after I pass their guard - it's way higher percentage than trying to break them down with traditional turtle attacks. The key is you have to be explosive with the entry but then immediately calm and controlled once you get both hooks in. What makes it work at the highest level is that it bypasses all the hand fighting and crossface battles that elite guys are prepared for from turtle. They're ready to defend their neck and fight grips, but most people haven't spent enough time defending leg-based turtle attacks, so you catch them by surprise. My favorite thing about Double Jump is how it forces reactions - the opponent has to choose between defending the back take or defending the truck entry, and both choices lead to dominant positions for you. In competition, I'm looking to establish this within 3-5 seconds of them hitting turtle, then immediately transitioning to either crab ride or full back control depending on how they react. The position has a short shelf life though - you can't hang out here, you have to capitalize immediately or they'll start defending intelligently.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Double Jump is pure 10th Planet methodology, man - we're using leg entanglements to create chaos and force the opponent into bad positions. This is what happens when you stop thinking about jiu-jitsu in terms of traditional gi-based controls and start asking 'how can I use my whole body as a weapon?' The beauty of Double Jump is it's basically saying 'fuck your turtle defense' because all those traditional turtle escapes and defensive postures don't work when someone has bilateral hooks controlling your hips. What I love teaching about this position is how it opens up the entire truck system and twister game. You're not just attacking for back control like traditional grappling - you're creating multiple submission threats through the truck, the twister, calf slicers, and then yeah, you can still take the back if you want. The position is all about creating uncertainty in the opponent's mind. They don't know if you're going to roll them into truck, drive them forward into crab ride, or just climb to back control. That mental pressure, combined with the physical control of the hooks, breaks people down faster than any amount of crossface pressure. When you train Double Jump, focus on the flow between positions rather than holding any one spot - it's a transition position that opens doors to everywhere you want to go.
